title: Mathematics and Statistics in the Era of Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytics
abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Data Analytics has transformed the landscape of science, engineering, business, healthcare, finance, and social sciences. At the heart of this transformation lie the fundamental disciplines of Mathematics and Statistics, which provide the theoretical foundations, computational techniques, and analytical frameworks that enable intelligent systems to learn, reason, predict, and make informed decisions. As we move towards an increasingly data-driven world, the integration of mathematical principles with statistical methodologies has become indispensable in addressing complex real-world challenges. The edited volume, "Mathematics and Statistics in the Era of Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytics: Foundations – Methods – Applications – Future," has been conceived with the objective of bringing together researchers, academicians, industry experts, and scholars to present recent developments and emerging trends at the intersection of mathematics, statistics, artificial intelligence, and data science. This book serves as a comprehensive platform for disseminating innovative research, theoretical advancements, computational methodologies, and practical applications that contribute to the rapidly expanding field of intelligent data-driven technologies. The emergence of AI has revolutionized the way data are collected, processed, interpreted, and utilized. Modern machine learning algorithms, deep learning architectures, optimization techniques, and intelligent decision-support systems rely heavily on mathematical modeling, statistical inference, probability theory, numerical methods, and computational algorithms. Likewise, data analytics has evolved from simple descriptive statistics to sophisticated predictive and prescriptive analytical frameworks capable of solving complex multidisciplinary problems. This convergence of mathematics, statistics, and artificial intelligence has opened new opportunities for scientific discovery, technological innovation, and societal development. Recognizing these developments, this volume encompasses a broad spectrum of contemporary topics that reflect both foundational theories and cutting-edge research. The book begins with Foundations of Mathematics for AI and Data Science, covering linear algebra, matrix computations, optimization techniques, differential equations, mathematical modeling, and scientific computing. These mathematical tools continue to serve as the backbone of artificial intelligence algorithms and computational intelligence systems. The second theme focuses on Statistical Foundations of Data Analytics, highlighting probability theory, random variables, statistical inference, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, predictive modeling, and multivariate statistical techniques. These concepts remain central to extracting meaningful information from complex datasets and ensuring reliable evidence-based decision-making. Another major component of the volume explores Machine Learning and Mathematical Frameworks, discussing supervised and unsupervised learning, optimization algorithms, statistical learning theory, feature selection, and dimensionality reduction techniques. These chapters bridge mathematical rigor with computational intelligence, demonstrating how theoretical concepts translate into practical machine learning applications. The volume further addresses Artificial Intelligence and Computational Intelligence, including neural networks, deep learning, fuzzy logic, intelligent systems, evolutionary computing, swarm intelligence, and reinforcement learning. These topics illustrate the remarkable advancements in intelligent computing that continue to reshape industrial automation, robotics, healthcare diagnostics, autonomous systems, and digital transformation. Given the unprecedented growth of digital information, the book also presents comprehensive discussions on Data Analytics and Big Data Technologies, emphasizing data preprocessing, data quality assessment, exploratory data analysis, big data analytics, visualization techniques, and interpretation of complex datasets. These methodologies are essential for transforming raw data into actionable knowledge across diverse application domains. Recognizing the importance of real-world implementation, several chapters focus on Mathematical and Statistical Modeling in AI Applications, including healthcare analytics, financial modeling, engineering optimization, industrial applications, environmental sustainability, and climate data analytics. These contributions demonstrate how mathematical and statistical models can effectively address practical challenges while supporting informed policy formulation and strategic decision-making. The editors have also included emerging research directions through dedicated sections on Advanced Topics in AI and Data Science, covering Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), quantum computing, graph theory, network analytics, and large language models. These chapters provide valuable insights into next-generation intelligent technologies that are expected to redefine scientific research and industrial innovation over the coming decades. In today's digital society, technological advancement must be accompanied by ethical responsibility. Therefore, the volume includes important discussions on Ethics, Security, and Responsible AI, addressing privacy-preserving data analytics, fairness, transparency, bias mitigation, governance frameworks, and ethical issues in AI-driven systems. Responsible innovation remains essential for building trustworthy intelligent technologies that benefit society while safeguarding individual rights and public interests. Finally, the book concludes with perspectives on Future Directions and Emerging Research, exploring AI-driven scientific discovery, mathematical challenges in next-generation artificial intelligence, interdisciplinary research opportunities, and future trends in data analytics and intelligent systems. These chapters aim to inspire researchers and students to pursue innovative ideas that contribute to sustainable technological advancement and scientific excellence. The editors sincerely believe that this volume will serve as a valuable reference for researchers, faculty members, postgraduate students, doctoral scholars, industry professionals, and policymakers working in mathematics, statistics, computer science, artificial intelligence, data science, engineering, economics, healthcare, and other interdisciplinary domains. The diverse collection of chapters reflects the richness of current research while encouraging collaboration across traditional disciplinary boundaries. We express our heartfelt gratitude to all the authors who contributed their original research, comprehensive reviews, and innovative ideas to this volume. Their scholarly efforts have significantly enriched the quality and scope of this book. We are equally thankful to the reviewers for their constructive comments, critical evaluations, and valuable suggestions, which have helped maintain the academic rigor and scientific quality of the published chapters. Our sincere appreciation is extended to the publisher for their unwavering support, professional guidance, and commitment to disseminating quality academic literature. We also acknowledge our colleagues, institutions, research collaborators, and family members for their encouragement and support throughout the preparation of this volume. It is our earnest hope that "Mathematics and Statistics in the Era of Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytics: Foundations – Methods – Applications – Future" will contribute meaningfully to the advancement of knowledge, stimulate innovative research, foster interdisciplinary collaboration, and inspire future generations of researchers to explore the limitless possibilities at the intersection of mathematics, statistics, artificial intelligence, and data analytics. title: Prediction-based sign placement using QA sampling
abstract: We present a pedestrian-flow forecasting and sign-placement workflow that leverages quantum annealing (QA) not as an optimizer, but as a sampler of individual trajectories. To reconstruct latent crowd dynamics from sparse measurements, we formulate a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model where the energy landscape encodes both physical validity (uniqueness) and transition preferences. By treating the annealer as a probabilistic sampler, we generate a diverse ensemble of feasible trajectories that are consistent with time-varying transition preferences derived from periodic headcounts. Aggregating these microscopic samples yields probabilistic macroscopic flow forecasts, which are then directly used to rank candidate links and guide the placement of temporary guidance signs. We evaluate this approach using simulated quantum annealing (SQA) and a physical D-Wave annealer. SQA results confirm the model’s validity, reproducing empirical congestion patterns with reasonable consistency and verifying that the QUBO formulation correctly captures crowd dynamics. In contrast, hardware QA exhibits a high rate (approximately 95%) of constraint violations. Crucially, we find that these violations occur despite a zero chain-break fraction, suggesting limits in the hardware’s effective dynamic range rather than connectivity failures. Although the repaired QA samples yielded an aggregate RMSE between observed and reconstructed proportions that is numerically close to the SQA baseline, the resulting flow structures were spatially incoherent. This near-equal RMSE conceals a qualitative breakdown. It arises because the randomized repair process statistically matches marginal densities while destroying the coherent flow structure that the QUBO’s transition preferences are designed to encode. A classical parallel-tempering sampler on the identical QUBO satisfies the same constraint essentially perfectly (violation rate \(<1\%\) ) at a slightly lower RMSE than SQA, indicating that the feasibility gap we observe is specific to the hardware rather than to the formulation. Our results indicate that simply increasing penalty strengths is insufficient due to hardware dynamic range limits; instead, a comprehensive recalibration of the penalty landscape is required.

title: GRAFT: Graph-Distilled Generative Retrieval for Facet-Aware Scientific Literature Exploration
abstract: Scientific papers may relate by problem, method, result, or contribution, but document-level retrievers collapse these into a single similarity score without saying why they are related. Citation- and similarity-based retrieval alone also confines search to the neighbourhood of what is already known, whereas generative retrieval generates document identifiers directly, enabling the exploratory retrieval that scientific discovery depends on. We connect papers in a graph whose edges are typed by these four facets, derived from facet items and citation signals, and distil it into a generative retriever whose identifiers are the papers' own facet text. Two graph properties do not survive naive distillation. First, because every training pair is an edge, naive enumeration indexes just 84% of the corpus. Coverage-aware distillation makes every paper learnable through a reverse-neighbour fallback, a minimum-coverage threshold, and edge-importance weighting. Second, constrained decoding guarantees that every generated identifier is a valid paper, but not that the graph connects it to the query. Graph-weighted reciprocal rank fusion scales each candidate's rank term by its query-candidate edge weight, dropping unsupported ones. On LitWeave, our constructed corpus of 11,359 NLP papers, Graft recovers 91% of its graph teacher's Recall@20 with no nearest-neighbour index or encoder at inference, and outperforms the graph teacher on query papers outside the corpus. It reproduces the graph's own facet labels at 0.922 precision, so every returned paper arrives labelled with the facet that surfaced it rather than an opaque score.

title: When Does Visual Generation Help Visual Understanding in Unified Multimodal Models?
abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) can perform both understanding and generation, raising a central question: can visual generation improve understanding? Existing evaluations provide mixed evidence, but confound task difficulty, reasoning paradigms, and the closed-loop interaction between generation and understanding. We introduce VGAU-Diag, a fine-grained evaluation framework for vision generation-assisted understanding. It stratifies samples by difficulty, enables unified evaluation of multiple reasoning paradigms, and uses Oracle-Assisted Reference Protocols. Our analysis shows that generated visual aids help on easier instances but become unreliable as reasoning complexity increases. Oracle-assisted diagnosis further reveals that the main bottleneck often lies on the visual-understanding side rather than the visual-generation side, as current UMMs struggle to leverage even faithful visual aids. We also show that effective visual generation should target visual-understanding bottlenecks rather than add more reasoning steps, and identify a three-stage transition from task-irrelevant noise, to misleading plausible guidance, and finally to useful assistance. These findings would be useful to guide the development of better UMMs.

title: Finite-ensemble observability of the mean-field convergence rate in consensus-based optimization
abstract: Consensus-based optimization (CBO) has a convergence guarantee for the implementable algorithm, assembled from a convergence result in mean-field law, aquantitative mean-field approximation and a discretization estimate. The guarantee is asymptotic in the ensemble size, and the constants carrying the parameterdependence sit in the prefactor rather than in the exponent. This paper asks anarrower question: which of those parameter dependencies are visible as effectson the slope fitted to a finite run, under experimental protocols that are statedand audited rather than assumed. Across 31320 coupled realizations distributedover 2 346 cells of 12 to 20 realizations each, we report four results.First, an inverse-temperature rule matched by objective spread produces anapparent dimension-dependent degradation of the fitted exponent of 0.96 fromd = 2 to d = 40. Calibrating the reference ensemble so that τ0,∞ =ESS0(J∞)/J∞ equals a target τ0, and fitting only over ensemble sizes J ≥1/τ0 at which that target is attainable, reduces it to 0.054, 0.059 and 0.078at τ0 = 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01. Both restrictions matter: a probe-calibrated fitover the full grid gives 0.030, 0.099 and 0.553, and the formal dimensionconcentration interaction that is resolved over the full grid, +0.0305 with interval[+0.0123,+0.0479], is not resolved over the restricted one, +0.0073 with[−0.0091,+0.0227].Second, the remaining contrast is confounded and we report it as such. Thenested subensembles whose error is measured are systematically further fromtheir concentration target at d = 40 than at d = 2 at every size measured.A dedicated experiment that controls finite-ensemble concentration exactly, atthe cost of one inverse temperature per ensemble size and therefore of changingthe algorithm along the fitted J-curve, does not make the contrast vanish but isinconclusive about the mechanism of the residual.Third, outside the parameter condition 2λ > dσ2 the onset is not resolvable fromthe boundary r = dσ2/(2λ) = 1, nine of ten bootstrap intervals containingit, while the severity is resolved: under the probe-calibrated protocol at nominal τ0 = 0.1,the non-admissible severity ˆγ(3)−ˆγ(1) grows at +0.144 per doublingof d with interval [+0.123,+0.164] for isotropic diffusion and at −0.002 with[−0.030,+0.027] for anisotropic. These experiments remain probe-calibratedat nominal τ0 = 0.1, and r is shown to move the concentration trajectory itself,so the effect is not orthogonal to concentration.Fourth, the parameter region in which the theorem applies and the region inwhich its exponent is visible in a finite run are different sets: admissible cells failthe operational criterion and non-admissible ones pass it. These finite-windowresults are not tests of, and do not contradict, the cited asymptotic convergencetheorems; every quantity measured is a finite-window fitted slope and not anasymptotic rate

title: K_mean Cluster
abstract: Dataset Description The dataset used in this Python-based K-Means exercise consists of 10,000 observations described by seven numerical variables, (X_1) through (X_7). Each observation is identified by a unique number, which serves only as an identifier and is not used as a clustering feature. Unlike supervised learning datasets, this dataset does not contain a predefined target or class variable. The purpose of the exercise is therefore to allow the K-Means algorithm to discover the underlying structure of the data and identify groups of observations based on their similarity across the seven numerical features. Because K-Means is a distance-based unsupervised learning algorithm, the scale and distribution of the variables must be examined before clustering. If the variables are measured on substantially different scales, features with larger numerical values may have a disproportionate influence on the Euclidean distance. Therefore, the dataset should first be explored for its dimensions, data types, missing values, and descriptive statistics, followed, when appropriate, by standardization of the numerical variables. After data preparation, K-Means will be applied for different values of K, and the resulting clustering solutions will be evaluated using measures such as WCSS and the Elbow Method to help identify an appropriate number of clusters. The final solution will then be analyzed through cluster assignments, centroid values, visualizations, and an interpretation of the characteristics of the resulting groups. Dataset Structure Variable Role id Unique observation identifier; not used for clustering (X_1) Numerical feature 1 (X_2) Numerical feature 2 (X_3) Numerical feature 3 (X_4) Numerical feature 4 (X_5) Numerical feature 5 (X_6) Numerical feature 6 (X_7) Numerical feature 7 The complete Python exercise will therefore follow the practical workflow: [\boxed{\text{Data Exploration}\rightarrow\text{Data Preparation}\rightarrow\text{Standardization}\rightarrow\text{Selection of } K\rightarrow\text{K-Means}\rightarrow\text{Cluster Assignment}\rightarrow\text{Centroids}\rightarrow\text{Visualization}\rightarrow\text{Interpretation}}] This structure allows students to move from the manual K-Means calculations in Part One to a realistic dataset containing 10,000 observations and seven variables, thereby connecting the mathematical foundations of clustering with its practical implementation in Python.
